description: I'm a 7th-semester student and work as an engineer by day. I built an ML project with cited, verifiable AI answers and now I'm applying that idea to farming. For Field Shift I'm building TEA: a tool that compares 3 crop rotations using NASA data (POWER, SMAP, GPM, NDVI), showing evidence, unknowns and risks for each. It supports farmers, never replaces them. Open to ideas, especially from agronomy or geospatial people.
summary: TEA-8 turns NASA climate, soil-moisture and vegetation data and USDA soil and crop records into evidence a farmer can check, with the source of every statement shown. For McLean County, Illinois, it compares three crop rotations side by side; anywhere else in the contiguous US, a farmer can draw their own field and get its dry summers, NDVI and VCI per summer, soils and crop history, plus a printable report. It gives no score and no "best option", says what the data cannot tell, and answers questions only from the data, with every claim checked by code.
details:
Problem. A dry summer can cut yields sharply, and a farmer choosing what to plant needs evidence, not a black-box recommendation. The Field Shift challenge asks for a tool that supports the decision without replacing farmer judgment or local expertise.

What it does.

• A year control (2001 to 2026) shows each summer's rainfall, temperature and root-zone soil moisture from NASA POWER, plus NASA GIBS MODIS vegetation (NDVI) on the map, so the change between dry and wet years is visible. The headline for a year says whether summer was drier than average.

• Three rotations are compared side by side, including the one in use today. Hypothetical rotations are labelled as hypothetical. For each: why it is suggested, what evidence supports it, what we do not know, and risks for a local expert to review.

• The farmer can state what matters most (water, soil or income). There is no final score and no "best option".

• An AI agent answers questions, but only from the project's data. A citation guard written in code checks every claim: it must cite evidence, every cited item must exist in the data, and every number must match the cited data. Claims that fail are shown as "Not verified". Example: the model wrote 23.3 °C for summer 2012 temperature; the data say 25.6 °C, and the guard caught it.

• Any place or field in the contiguous US: paste coordinates, click the map or draw a field on the aerial photo. The tool queries NASA POWER, NASA MODIS, USDA SSURGO and CropScape live and shows the dry summers of the area, how green each summer was (NDVI) and how it ranks against the other summers (VCI, 0 to 100), the soils inside the field with their share, and the crop of each year since 2008. Questions about that field go through the same citation guard. A link reopens the same field, and a printable English report gathers the map, charts, color scales, limits and sources.

• A "What we do not know" panel lists data gaps (for example, county yields cover corn and soybeans as a whole, so the comparison measures stress and exposure, not yield outcomes per rotation) and limits (NASA POWER is a grid of about 50 km that represents the area, not the plot).

How it works. For McLean County, data are prepared in Python and served as static JSON. For any other place or field, a Python service on Google Cloud Run queries the sources live, with time limits so a slow service does not hold the answer. The web app is React with Vite and Leaflet on Vercel. Questions go through a small service on Google Cloud Run that calls the language model, then runs the citation guard before anything is shown.

Limits, stated in the tool. The rotation comparison and county yields are for one county; other places get no rotations and no yields. For a drawn field, climate is a cell of about 50 km, NDVI and VCI one 250 m pixel, and crops a few points inside the field. Not agronomic advice. No yield claim per rotation. Satellite and ground measurements differ, and the tool explains terms such as NDVI and soil moisture.

Future. County yields for any place; crop shares over the whole field instead of sample points; real yields by crop from USDA NASS QuickStats; alternative crops checked with local trials; farmer-entered constraints such as water, equipment and market.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

• Claude (Anthropic), via Claude Code: research on the challenge and sources, tests of the data APIs, code and text drafts, the demo video assembly. Everything it produced was reviewed by the team member who signs the project.

• Muse Spark (Meta Model API): answers questions at runtime from the project's data; every claim is checked by code against the data before it is shown.

• ElevenLabs text-to-speech (free plan): the AI-generated voice-over of the demo video. Audio notice also in the video's metadata.

• Music and sound effects: HyperFrames / HeyGen audio catalog (not generated by the team).

• The idea for the solution (comparison of rotations with visible evidence, gaps and a citation guard) is the team's.

Inspiration

Style inspiration only, no code or images reused: NASA Worldview, Space Apps 2025 winners (Queñaris, Henry's Farm Adventures, Twisters), author's earlier hackathon project Ether (layout idea, and the idea of a deterministic citation check; code written from scratch).
